failure_modes: Consistent co‑isolation artifact: immuno-capture or fractionation reproducibly enriches non‑vesicular particles (lipoproteins, protein aggregates) so the multi‑omic fingerprint is specific to a contaminant class rather than EVs (false positive identity signal).

Insufficient analytic sensitivity / low biomass: capture-positive, detergent/protease‑protected fractions have too little material for reliable multi‑omic measurement, producing noisy, nonreproducible profiles or false negatives that confound similarity metrics.

Assay-induced artifacts: protease/detergent treatments, capture elution buffers, or spike‑ins differentially affect recovery across molecular classes, producing artifactual detergent-sensitivity patterns or apparent membrane protection that do not reflect in‑situ EV biology.

Labeling / capture‑reagent bias: choice of capture reagent (tetraspanin vs TIM4/AnxA5) selectively enriches distinct particle subpopulations (or co‑enriches bound secretome complexes), so cross‑lot “consistency” is method‑dependent and not generalizable across capture methods or to in vivo function.

Downstream processing damage: manufacturing or formulation exposures selectively destroy membrane‑protected cargo in some lots (or during storage), creating lot‑to‑lot variability that reflects process sensitivity rather than biologically meaningful differences—leading to false negatives or over‑stringent rejection.

Cross‑species translation limit: biodistribution and functional relevance of captured EV cargo may not map to clinically relevant delivery or potency (e.g., intranasal rodent efficacy vs. negligible intranasal macaque brain uptake), so an EV‑centric fingerprint may not predict in vivo performance or de‑risk translational outcomes.

Overfitting to limited lots: deriving a fingerprint from only ≥3 matched lots risks identifying process‑specific but not source‑general signatures; the metric may fail when scaled to broader donor/passage variability or alternate manufacturing runs.

Inadequate controls: inability to run sufficiently informative secretome-only, positive EV, and spike‑in controls (or to show that captured signals are detergent/protease‑sensitive) will leave ambiguity whether signals arise from membrane protection or soluble/co‑isolated material.
strongest_objection: The most bounded and plausible failure is that the candidate “protected” multi-omic fingerprint actually reflects reproducible co‑isolation of non‑vesicular secretome components or assay artifacts (e.g., lipoproteins, protein aggregates, or capture-reagent-associated contaminants) rather than bona fide membrane-enclosed EV cargo; because such co-isolates can be consistently carried through matched upstream processes, the assay would report a stable cross‑lot signature that is not specific to intact EVs and therefore would mislead downstream lot‑gating and translational inferences.
